message:
Please read this carefully:

<document>
# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

</document>
response:
This is a much stronger study than the Halden pilot. It fixes most of the problems I raised there:
- It has a randomised control group and a registered protocol.
- Output comes from administrative records rather than manager ratings.
- Actual hours come from timesheets, and the authors explicitly reject the inflated per-scheduled-hour figure.
- It reports the coverage-bound result honestly instead of folding it into a "sector-general" claim.
- The exploratory analysis is clearly labelled as such.

The arithmetic checks out:
- Case-processing: 0.979 / 0.87 ≈ 1.125, so +12.5% per actual hour. Against scheduled hours, 0.979 / 0.8 ≈ 1.224, the 22% the authors cite.
- Counter: 0.886 / 0.83 ≈ 1.067, so +6.7%.
- Actual hours: 37.9 → 33.0 is −12.9%, and 37.6 → 31.2 is −17.0%.

The issues below are about the remaining weak points, roughly in order of importance.

## 1. Possible spillover between treated and control offices

The design assumes that what happens in one office doesn't affect another. Two features of county administration could break that:
- **Telephone routing.** Contact-centre systems often route calls to whichever centre has capacity. If so, calls the understaffed treated centres couldn't answer would flow to control centres. Treated output would fall and control output would rise, which roughly doubles the measured gap.
- **Shared case queues.** If cases can be reassigned between case-processing offices, managers may have moved work from treated to control offices to protect deadlines.

The paper should say whether queues and call routing are office-specific. If they aren't, it should report total county output and whether control offices' incoming work changed during the trial. As written, the counter result in particular could be partly a redistribution effect.

## 2. Only 10 offices in the counter stratum

Clustered standard errors are unreliable with so few clusters (5 v 5 in the counter stratum, 7 v 7 in case-processing) and usually come out too narrow. The interval of −16.9 to −5.9 for counter output may therefore be optimistic, and the per-hour interval of +0.4 to +13.3, which barely excludes zero, could easily cross it.

I'd ask for wild cluster bootstrap or randomisation-inference p-values alongside the reported intervals. With 24 offices, randomisation inference is easy to run and directly reflects the design.

## 3. The counter per-hour gain is probably just busier staff

When work is driven by demand, contacts handled per hour depend mainly on how much of the time staff are busy. With fewer staff on duty, queues lengthen and staff are idle less often. Handled contacts per hour then rise automatically, which matches the wait rising from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes.

So "each hour worked was somewhat more productive" may not mean anyone worked faster. It may only mean less slack. Handling time per contact, if the telephony system records it, would distinguish the two explanations. I'd soften the wording until that's checked.

## 4. The counter output loss is only partly explained

If demand stayed the same, abandoned calls rising from 6% to 10% would cut contacts handled by about 4%: the share served falls from 94% to 90%. The measured fall is 11.4%. The paper should explain the remaining roughly 7 points. Possible causes:
- calls rerouted to other centres (see §1),
- people deterred from contacting the service, or moving to other channels,
- in-person visitors leaving the queue without being served.

This affects how the "loss of service" is understood. Rerouted calls, deterred contacts and lost contacts are very different outcomes for the public.

## 5. Results reported inconsistently with the stated difference-in-differences design

- **Waiting time and abandoned calls** are shown only as before-and-after figures for treated offices, without a control comparison. Abandonment is also not in the registered list of outcomes and should be labelled as unregistered.
- **Quality** ("3.1% v 3.0%", "11.8% v 10.9%") has no confidence interval. It's unclear whether these are levels or difference-in-differences estimates. The repeat-contact rate rose in counter offices, and the text doesn't mention it.
- **Sick days** are reported pooled across both strata with no interval, although they were a registered outcome. Report them by stratum. Counter staff facing longer queues may not have benefited equally.
- **Resignations** (3.9% v 7.4%) are a level comparison and don't appear in the registered outcomes. Label them exploratory.

## 6. "No loss of output" isn't actually shown for case-processing

The interval of −6.8% to +2.6% is consistent with no effect. It is also consistent with a loss of nearly 7%. The county's question was whether the change could happen "without loss of service", which is a non-inferiority question.

Unless the protocol set an acceptable margin of loss in advance, the paper can't claim the absence of a loss. It can only say a loss larger than about 7% is unlikely. If the margin was pre-specified, report against it.

## 7. Further issues in case-processing

- **Overtime cost.** Staff kept full pay and also claimed about 3 hours of overtime a week: scheduled hours were 30 and actual hours 33.0. The paper should report cost per case closed. If overtime is paid at a premium, cost per case rose even though output barely moved. Also report how overtime was distributed across staff. If a few people carried most of it, that has consequences for workload and sustainability.
- **Unclaimed work.** Timesheets record only claimed overtime. Case work done from home or off the clock wouldn't appear, so the fall in actual hours could be overstated, and the per-hour gain with it.
- **Case mix.** "Cases closed" doesn't account for difficulty. Treated offices might have prioritised quick cases, which would show up later as a growing or ageing backlog. The authors raise deadline risk only as a future concern, but backlog size, backlog age and deadline breaches can already be reported at nine months.
- **Appeal timing.** Decisions made late in the trial won't have been appealed yet. The overturn rate mostly reflects decisions from early in the trial and may be incomplete.

## 8. The meetings analysis is weaker than its framing suggests

The authors are already cautious, but two points are missing:
- **No baseline.** Meeting data were collected only in month six. The 3.8 v 7.1 hours difference could have existed before the trial, so it can't be attributed to treatment.
- **The correlation is not significant.** With seven offices, r = 0.71 has a 95% interval of roughly −0.09 to 0.95 (p ≈ 0.07).

The Summary's "may account for part of the gain" is acceptable given the caveats in the body. It's still worth adding "unregistered" in the Summary itself. Readers who see only the Summary will remember the mechanism, not the caveats.

## 9. Smaller points

- **Balance and pre-trends.** Add a table of baseline balance by stratum and show the pre-period trends that support the difference-in-differences comparison.
- **Staff per stratum.** Give staff numbers per stratum, not just the total of 1,180, and say how part-time staff were handled in the FTE figures.
- **Effort effects in the control group.** The limitations mention that control staff knew a trial was under way. Under the trial, control output could have been lowered by resentment or raised by competitiveness. Either would bias the comparison. Spell this out.
- **Who requested the meeting data.** It was collected "at the request of office managers", who may have had a view on the result. The paper should note this.
- **Policy implication for counters.** The Discussion could state it directly: in coverage-bound work, keeping service levels on a shorter week requires more staff, which costs money. Even a rough estimate of that cost would make the policy conclusion concrete.

## Overall

The main conclusions are well supported:
- Per-hour and per-employee productivity diverge.
- Productivity measured against scheduled hours overstates the gain.
- Coverage-bound work behaves differently.

The points most likely to change the numbers are spillover between offices (§1) and inference with few clusters (§2). The ones most likely to change the interpretation are the busier-staff explanation for the counter per-hour gain (§3) and the unexplained part of the counter output loss (§4).

I can draft a reviewer report from these notes or a revised Summary paragraph.
